title: Prevalence of intimate partner violence against women in East Africa: A systematic review and meta-analysis
content:
by Zekarias Markos, Esubalew Muluneh Aligaz, Sitotaw Tesfa Zegeye, Rahel Dinkneh, Temesgen Mamo, Sintayehu Samuel Lorato

Background

Intimate partner violence (IPV) remains a pervasive public health and human rights issue worldwide, with sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) bearing a disproportionately high burden. However, synthesized evidence specifically from the East African region is limited.

Methods

A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted following PRISMA guidelines. Forty-one cross-sectional studies reporting IPV among women in East Africa were identified from seven electronic databases (PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, African Journals Online [AJOL], CINAHL, and Google Scholar). Databases were searched from August 1 to September 30, 2025.Study quality was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal checklist for prevalence studies. A random-effects inverse-variance model was used to estimate pooled prevalence with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Heterogeneity was assessed using the I2 statistic. Subgroup analyses were performed by country, population, study setting, recall period, IPV type, publication year, sample size, and data collection tool. Publication bias was assessed via funnel plots, Egger’s test, and the trim-and-fill method. Sensitivity analysis was conducted using leave-one-out procedures.

Results

The meta-analysis included 41 studies. The overall pooled prevalence of IPV was 42.8% (95% CI: 38.3–47.9%), indicating high heterogeneity (I2 = 99.6%). Subgroup analyses revealed significant variation: the highest prevalence was among contraceptive users (72.6%, based on a single study) and ever-married/partnered women (55.1%), while the lowest was among refugees (31.0%) and in large-scale studies (32.9%). Country-level estimates were highest in Uganda (52.0%), followed by Tanzania (49.9%) and Ethiopia (44.5%), and lowest in Rwanda (20.9%). Studies using WHO standard tools reported higher prevalence (49.1%) than those using DHS modules (36.3%) No significant publication bias was detected (Egger’s test *p* = 0.284).Subgroup analyses revealed statistically significant between-group differences (p < 0.05) for country, study setting, and population subgroups, but not for measurement tool (p = 0.068).

Conclusion

This meta-analysis confirms a high prevalence of IPV among women in East Africa, with substantial variation across subpopulations, countries, and methodological factors. Findings highlight the need for targeted, context-specific interventions and the importance of standardized measurement tools in surveillance and research.
